learn.title: Functions get copies
learn.body: C passes arguments by value. A function receives copies of the numbers you give it, so changing them does not change your variables. To let a function change your data, give it the address instead.

learn.title: A swap that fails
learn.body: This prints `3 8`. `a` and `b` are copies, so swapping them changes nothing outside the function.

learn.title: A swap that works
learn.body: Pass addresses and write through them. Calling `swap(&x, &y);` and then printing x and y gives `8 3`.

learn.title: NULL means nothing
learn.body: `NULL` is a pointer value that points at nothing. Use it for "no address yet". Test with `if (p == NULL)` before using a pointer you are not sure about. Dereferencing `NULL` is undefined behavior; on common systems the program stops with a segmentation fault.

learn.title: Meeting a segfault
steps: `*p` tries to read memory the program may not use
The program usually crashes with Segmentation fault

learn.body: A segmentation fault is the system stopping a program that touched memory it should not. It is a symptom, so look for a bad pointer.

questions.prompt: Why does `bad(x, y)` not swap x and y?
questions.explanation: Arguments are copied, so the original variables stay unchanged.

questions.prompt: What must you pass so a function can change `x`?
questions.explanation: With the address, the function can write to where `x` lives.

questions.prompt: After `swap(&x, &y);` with `x = 3` and `y = 8`, what is x then y? Write it like `1 2`.
questions.explanation: The values were exchanged through the pointers.

questions.prompt: A pointer that points at nothing holds \_\_.
What usually happens when you dereference `NULL`?
questions.explanation: It is undefined behavior; a crash is the common result, but not guaranteed.
Test the pointer itself, not what it points at, before using it.

questions.prompt: Put the lines of `swap` in order.
questions.explanation: Save one value first, or it would be overwritten and lost.
